1) Ads for selling bank accounts (mule accounts) >> On the internet you can easily find ads such as “We buy/sell personal or corporate bank accounts,” offering to buy and sell bankbooks, cash/check cards, security cards, OTPs, etc. (collectively, “access media”) for KRW 800,000 to 3,000,000 per item. However, such account‑trading advertisements are regulated under the Electronic Financial Transactions Act. Acts of brokering/mediating/advertising the sale of access media, or recommending such transactions while receiving, demanding, or promising consideration are prohibited by law (Electronic Financial Transactions Act, Art.6(3)5). “Access media” means the means or information used to issue transaction instructions or to ensure authenticity and accuracy of users and transactions in electronic financial transactions, including: electronic cards or equivalent electronic information; electronic signature creation information and certificates; user IDs registered with financial institutions or electronic financial businesses; biometric information; and passwords required to use such media or information.

2) “Work‑loan” advertisements >> Ads such as “Loans available to anyone regardless of credit” or “custom credit loans” are so‑called “work‑loan” ads—fraudulent schemes in which loan applicants’ information is forged or falsified to deceive financial institutions. (Source: FSS press release, “College‑aged youth should beware of scam ‘work‑loan’ offers.”)

Types of work‑loans include:
- Work‑loans to obtain jeonse or business funds by registering a business: forging or falsifying lease contracts or business registrations
- High‑amount work‑loans to raise limits by fabricating income certificates or payroll transfer records
- Work‑loans requiring a guarantor: forging documents and setting a guarantor unrelated to the borrower
- Work‑loans for the unemployed or low‑credit borrowers: forging employment certificates, income verification, etc., under the pretext of raising credit scores

3) Ads by unlicensed/unregistered lenders >> On the internet you may see ads such as “same‑day loan approval for anyone” or “emergency cash loans.” These are likely from unlicensed or unregistered lenders targeting vulnerable groups such as low‑credit borrowers and students. Anyone wishing to operate a lending or loan‑brokerage business (excluding financial institutions) must register each business office with the relevant metropolitan mayor, governor, or special‑self‑governing province governor (Act on Registration of Credit Business and Protection of Financial Users, Art.3(1)). Therefore, before using a lender, you should first verify whether it is a registered business. Also, unless one is a registered lender or a financial institution, one must not advertise lending business (Act on Registration of Credit Business and Protection of Financial Users, Art.9‑2(1)). Registered lender information can be checked on each city/province website or via the Financial Supervisory Service website (Consumer Protection → Seomin Finance 1332 → Financial Company Search → Registered Lenders).

4) Advertising through name theft >> In internet or SMS ads, there are cases where people mislead consumers by stealing or using similar names of famous banks. This is regulated by the Act on Fair Labeling and Advertising. Businesses must not engage in, or cause others to engage in, misleading advertising that can deceive consumers or distort fair trade, including:
- False/exaggerated advertising: advertising contrary to facts or excessively inflating facts
- Deceptive advertising: concealing or minimizing facts
- Unfair comparative advertising: comparing with other companies or products without clearly stating the comparison target and criteria or without objective grounds, and claiming superiority
- Defamatory advertising: disparaging others with unfounded content or only presenting unfavorable facts

□ Common

☞ Exposure time: For broadcast ads via media specified in §2(1)(a) (excluding radio), indicate exposure time (unit: seconds).
☞ Review: “○” compliant, “×” non‑compliant, “△” insufficient, “–” not applicable.

Checklist items (relevant laws: Money‑Lending Business Act, Financial Consumer Protection Act, related enforcement decrees):

1) Business name or representative name
- Display at the top‑left of the ad
- Use a font size at least one‑third of the largest font in the ad
- Make it larger than the trademark text and easily recognizable

2) Product name
- State the financial product name
- For broadcast ads, show subtitles for at least one‑fifth of total ad time

3) Loan conditions
- Include the consumer’s required credit conditions and repayment method, etc.
- Colors/sizes/speech speed should balance benefits and disadvantages to consumers

4) Interest rate and delinquency interest rate
- Display clearly; distinguishable from other ad elements
- Use a font size at least one‑third of the largest font
- Show the range and calculation basis and timing of interest charges
- Colors/sizes/speech speed should balance benefits and disadvantages

5) Ancillary fees
- Display ancillary fees other than interest
- Use size comparable to the company name and distinguishable from other items
- For broadcast ads, subtitles for at least one‑fifth of total ad time

6) Business address
- If there are two or more offices in different cities/provinces, only the head office address may be shown
- No restriction on location or font size

7) Advertising phone number
- Must be the phone number registered in the registry as the advertising phone number
- If there are two or more offices in different cities/provinces, only the head‑office advertising phone number may be shown
- Use size comparable to the company name and distinguishable from other items
- For broadcast ads, subtitles for at least one‑fifth of total ad time

8) Registration authority
- Name of the registering city/province or the Financial Supervisory Service
- No restriction on location or font size

(Continuation)

9) Registration
- Indicate that registration information for the relevant city/province or the Financial Supervisory Service can be confirmed
- No restriction on location or font size

10) Early repayment conditions
- Indicate the prepayment fee rate or conditions for early repayment (if there is no early‑repayment fee, state “no early‑repayment condition”)
- No restriction on location or font size

11) Warning phrase for excessive borrowing
- Choose one of the following phrases:
  “Excessive debt is the beginning of suffering.”
  “Excessive debt can bring you great misfortune.”
  “Excessive debt is a shortcut to bankruptcy.”
- Use size comparable to the company name and distinguishable from other items
- Use a font size at least one‑third of the largest font
- For broadcast ads, subtitles for at least one‑fifth of total ad time
- Print ads under 150 cm² may omit

12) Warning phrase for credit‑score decline
- Must state that if borrowing exceeds repayment ability or credit‑card use is excessive, personal credit scores may decline, causing disadvantages in financial transactions
- Choose one of the following phrases:
  “When you take out a loan, your credit rating or personal credit score may decline.”
  “When you take out a loan, a decline in credit rating or personal credit score may restrict other financial transactions.”
- Use size comparable to the company name and distinguishable from other items
- Use a font size at least one‑third of the largest font
- For broadcast ads, subtitles for at least one‑fifth of total ad time
- Print ads under 150 cm² may omit

13) Obligation to repay principal and interest upon delinquency
- Indicate that if scheduled principal/interest payments become delinquent for a certain period, all principal and interest may become due before maturity

14) Encourage reading product description and terms
- Include a statement encouraging consumers to read the financial product description and terms before concluding a contract

5. Online advertising review principles

A. Common standards

- The company must not make key information that could affect a consumer’s rational decision difficult to find in the advertisement, and should provide it on the same page where possible.

- The company must not intentionally make information unfavorable to consumers difficult to recognize. If the advertised benefits are not general or have exceptions, the corresponding constraints (disadvantages) must be displayed at the same level.

- If the linked online page for a product ad is the company’s homepage main screen or a similar page, the company must ensure consumers can easily find information about the product.

- If a company’s image advertisement links to a page containing product information, it is considered a loan advertisement and must comply with the loan‑ad review procedure and standards.

- If ad content changes, the ad must be promptly reviewed and revised in accordance with the rules to maintain currency, unless the ad clearly indicates it is valid only for a specific period.

B. Type‑specific standards

- Website ads
  The company’s advertising website (including mobile websites) must display all disclosure items required by Article 18 on the first screen in an easily recognizable manner.

- Viral ads
  When advertising through a person’s review or testimonial, the post must clearly indicate any economic interest (e.g., that the post was written in exchange for compensation from a lender).
  The disclosure must be displayed at the beginning or end of each post, distinct from the body text, and in a manner easily recognized by consumers (larger font size or different color, etc.).

  [Examples] Standard phrases
  - “I received economic compensation (cash, gift cards, fees, points, free products, etc.) from Company XX for recommending/introducing/promoting Product XX.”
  - “Paid advertisement,” “Sponsored advertisement,” or other expressions that clearly indicate an economic interest (when character limits apply)

  * The standard phrase must be placed at the beginning or end of each post and distinguishable from the body text, with larger font size or different color (see FTC Guidelines on Display and Advertising of Recommendations/Endorsements).

- Online banner ads
  As a rule, review should cover both the banner and the linked landing page.
  Except when the banner area is excessively limited, the advertiser’s name and product name should be stated within the banner itself rather than only on the linked page.

1. Key contents of the “Financial Advertising Regulation Guidelines”

Refer to the attached “Financial Advertising Regulation Guidelines” for details.

A. Scope of advertising regulation

- Under the Financial Consumer Protection Act, advertising is divided into “advertising about financial products” and “advertising about the business of financial product sellers/advisers.”
- Advertising under the Act means conduct that informs or presents matters about financial products or related business to the public (Act on Fair Labeling and Advertising applies).
- For example, if advertising‑like press releases about financial products or business are posted in public spaces such as a website, they can be regarded as advertising.
- Image advertising by financial companies is not subject to regulation.
- Broadcasts providing financial information can also be considered advertising under the Act.

If a broadcast directly or indirectly provides information about a specific seller’s product, it can be considered “financial product advertising.” However, if information is provided without sales intent and in a way that consumers cannot easily infer the product or seller (e.g., “Company A,” “Product B”), it may not be considered advertising.

Broadcasts that introduce a seller’s services and induce financial transactions are “business advertising.” Even if a specific service is not explicitly introduced, a broadcast designed to promote a specific company’s business may be considered business advertising.

Advertising regulation does not apply to non‑financial services that are incidental to a financial company’s business (e.g., a credit‑card company’s used‑car platform ad or an insurer’s healthcare ad).

B. Advertising主体 and procedures

The Financial Consumer Protection Act (Art.22(1)) strictly limits advertising by persons who are not financial product sellers (direct sellers, sales agents/brokers, advisers).

- Online portals and fintech firms are not merely “advertising media” but can be considered “advertising主体” if they actively intervene in the sales process; in such cases they must register as financial product sellers.

Financial product sellers must conduct (1) internal review and, depending on the sector, (2) pre‑review by an association when necessary.

- Associations legally recognized for financial sectors can conduct pre‑review, and may set their own scope and standards.
- For financial product sales agents/brokers, advertising requires confirmation from the direct seller of the product (if the ad contains products from multiple direct sellers, confirmation must be obtained from each).
- When advertising via online media such as blogs or YouTube, the ad must indicate that the direct seller has confirmed it.
- Business advertising does not require direct seller confirmation.

c. Matters related to advertising content and methods

When advertising, not only the Financial Consumer Protection Act but also other laws such as the Act on Fair Labeling and Advertising, the Broadcasting Act, and the Money-Lending Business Act must be checked to avoid violations.

* Financial Consumer Protection Act Article 6 (relationship with other laws): Unless otherwise specially provided by other laws concerning financial consumer protection, matters are governed by this Act.

In particular, for online media such as YouTube and blogs, advertisers should comply with the Fair Trade Commission’s revised “Guidelines on the Display and Advertising of Recommendations/Endorsements” to prevent hidden advertising (e.g., when celebrities advertise without disclosing economic ties with the advertiser).

Items that must be included in ads under the Financial Consumer Protection Act can be operated flexibly within the limits of the regulatory intent, considering the purpose and characteristics of the advertising medium. Because advertising is not the contract stage, it is not necessary to explain products in the same detail as the duty to explain; however, information should not be omitted arbitrarily in a way that may cause consumer misunderstanding.

For online banner and pop‑up ads where the advertising area is limited, it is possible to split and post advertising content across linked web pages.

Items mandated by statute (e.g., Financial Consumer Protection Act Art.22(3)1–3) cannot be omitted from advertisements.

The Financial Consumer Protection Act provides broad discretion regarding advertising methods (text, video, audio), but requires that the color/size of text and the speed/volume of audio be composed so that benefits and disadvantages are conveyed in a balanced manner.

Financial product sellers should reflect advertising standards in internal control standards, referencing association review criteria and cited cases. Associations can report violations discovered during pre‑review to the Financial Services Commission.
